title: Crush Runs of k Equal Letters
statement:
You get a string s and a number k. A crush picks k equal letters standing next to each other and deletes them; the pieces on either side close the gap. Keep crushing while any crush is possible.

Return the final string. It is the same whichever crushes you pick first.

examples.why: Crushing "bbb" leaves "aac". Only two a's meet, which is short of 3, so it stops.
Crushing "yyy" makes the lone x meet "xx". That new run of three x's is crushed too.
A crush removes exactly k letters. The fourth a stays.

hints: After a crush, which letters can suddenly become neighbours? Do you need to look anywhere else?
Process letters left to right and keep what survives so far. A new letter can only join the run at the very end of what you kept.
Keep a stack of [letter, count] runs. Push or extend the top run; when its count reaches k, pop it. The letters before it are now the end again, ready to merge with whatever comes next.

explain.intuition:
Simulating crushes one at a time means rescanning the string after each one, which is slow. Notice that a crush only ever joins the letters just left of it with the letters just right of it. So read the string from left to right and keep the part that has survived so far. A new letter can only extend the last run of the kept part.

Store the kept part as a stack of runs, each a letter and a count. A new letter either increments the top count or pushes a new run. When a count reaches k, pop the run: the run below becomes the top again and will merge with the next equal letter. Example 2 is exactly this chain reaction. It is the same pattern as matching brackets, with a counter instead of a pair.
steps: Create an empty stack of [letter, count].
For each letter: if the top run has the same letter, increase its count; otherwise push [letter, 1].
If the top count is now k, pop it.
At the end, write out each run's letter count times, bottom to top.
pitfalls: Removing the whole run when it is longer than k. Only k letters go; "aaaa" with k = 3 leaves one a.
Doing one left-to-right pass of deletions without a stack. Crushes create new runs (example 2) that a single scan never revisits.
Storing single letters and counting the run by walking down the stack each time. That costs O(k) per letter.

solutions.title: Crush and rescan
solutions.idea: Find any run of k equal letters, cut it out, and repeat until none is left.

solutions.title: Stack of runs
solutions.idea: Keep surviving letters as [letter, count] runs; pop a run as soon as its count reaches k.

followups: k = 2 and letters come one at a time from a live text field. How do you show the crushed text after each keystroke?
A crush now removes any run of k or more equal letters, whole. Does the stack still work, and what changes?
